item.title: Lula, Bolsonaro rally supporters on final day before Brazil presidential runoff
item.description: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday ahead of Sunday's presidential runoff vote, mobilizing supporters and making a final push for undecided voters.
item.dc:creator: Fernando Cardoso, Sebastian Rocandio, Lais Morais
item.content:encoded: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday ahead of Sunday's presidential runoff vote, mobilizing supporters and making a final push for undecided voters. The two candidates have remained neck and neck in polls following a [USN:L6N45Q04L TEXT:"stronger-than-expected"] performance by the right-wing senator in the first round. On Saturday, a [USN:S0N46101P TEXT:"CNT/MDA poll showed"] the senator with a 1.3-point lead. Lula, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, kicked off his last day of campaigning with a march along Rio de Janeiro's iconic Copacabana beach, where thousands of supporters joined the leftist incumbent under a blazing sun. "We're going to win the election for one simple reason: it's true that the people want change, (but) they want to move forward. They don't want to go backward," Lula told journalists before the rally. Later, the president led another march in Sao Paulo, passing along Paulista Avenue, a traditional venue for political demonstrations in Brazil's largest city. "It's so exciting to see everyone here. This is the kind of energy we want for Brazil. Brazil is ours," said Gisele Passos, a 61-year-old businesswoman at the Sao Paulo rally. For many Lula supporters, the rallies carried a bittersweet undertone. The 80-year-old president and former union leader is widely expected to be making his final bid for office, lending the campaign's closing events the feel of a farewell tour. "He's one of a kind. He has had an incredible, remarkable, and hard-fought journey. We're very proud of that," said Olga Leal, a 62-year-old retiree in Sao Paulo. BOLSONARO RALLIES IN BATTLEGROUND STATE Bolsonaro, meanwhile, joined a motorcycle caravan in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, a key battleground state. No candidate has won the presidency without carrying Minas Gerais since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s. The senator led Lula by around 5 percentage points in the state in the first round. "The time is almost here. There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years," said the lawmaker, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, in a social media video. He later took part in a campaign march in his home state of Rio de Janeiro, which he has represented in the Senate since 2019. The younger Bolsonaro was first backed by his father to run for the presidency last December. The former president was sentenced to over 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula. On Friday, Lula and Bolsonaro met for a [USN:L1N46A011 TEXT:"final debate"] on TV Globo, the country's main free-to-air television channel, where they sparred over the cost of living and traded personal attacks.

item.title: Alvarez apologises for Barcelona comments after scoring Atletico winner
item.description: Julian Alvarez gave Atletico Madrid supporters a winning goal and an apology on Saturday, sealing a 1-0 victory over Deportivo La Coruna before seeking forgiveness for declaring his desire to play for Barcelona.
item.dc:creator: Fernando Kallas
item.content:encoded: Julian Alvarez gave Atletico Madrid supporters a winning goal and an apology on Saturday, sealing a 1-0 victory over Deportivo La Coruna before seeking forgiveness for declaring his desire to play for Barcelona. The Argentine striker scored for the second successive match as Atletico moved within two points of LaLiga leaders Barca, then addressed the comments that had soured his relationship with fans at the Metropolitano. "I'd like to apologise to our fans for what I said at the World Cup; it was a mistake in terms of how I said it and the timing," Alvarez told Spanish broadcaster Movistar Plus. "I understand why the fans are angry. If I were a fan, I'd be angry too. Especially given how they've supported me since I arrived." Alvarez said during the 2026 World Cup that he "wanted to fulfil his dream" of playing for Barcelona, triggering a transfer dispute that stretched through pre-season and the summer window as [USN:L6N44O15D TEXT:"Atletico refused to sell "]to their rivals. Regularly booed at home this season, Alvarez received a standing ovation from some supporters after Saturday's goal. "I hope that with hard work and humility I can turn this situation around," he said. "I've been feeling better in recent matches – both physically and on the ball. I want to help the team and give my best." Second-placed Atletico have 25 points. Real Madrid, third with 21, visit Barcelona at Camp Nou on Sunday for the season's first Clasico.

item.title: Volkanovski keeps promise with quick win over Evloev at UFC 333
item.description: Australian Alexander Volkanovski retained his UFC featherweight title with a second-round technical knockout of Movsar Evloev at UFC 333 on Saturday, ending the Russian's unbeaten 20-fight professional run and keeping a promise to his wife.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australian Alexander Volkanovski retained his UFC featherweight title with a second-round technical knockout of Movsar Evloev at UFC 333 on Saturday, ending the Russian's unbeaten 20-fight professional run and keeping a promise to his wife. A thunderous combination sent Evloev backing up against the cage and Volkanovski followed him to the canvas before landing a series of unanswered blows that caused referee Marc Goddard to call off the fight with six seconds remaining in the frame. "It feels good to get a finish - I actually promised the missus, it was our wedding anniversary on Wednesday, I promised her a quick one so she wasn't stressing on the sideline, so there you go," he said grinning at his post-fight interview. The 38-year-old twice champion got through the first round without suffering too much damage and began to make his presence felt with precise striking in the second round, briefly sending Evloev to the canvas with a glancing blow to his temple. Evloev, 32, did his best to leverage his superior grappling but had no answer to Volkanovski's shrewd fighting style, which has been honed in a string of performances in title fights that have led pundits to consider him the best-ever featherweight. "I feel the love ... thank you so much. I really do appreciate it, I feel it from everyone, from the UFC staff, the fighters, every fan. The love that I get is just incredible, and I'm so thankful for it, so thank you all," he said. In the co-main event at The Etihad Arena on Yas Island, Russia's Petr Yan retained his bantamweight crown with a unanimous decision over Georgian Merab Dvalishvili in a battle fought at a frenetic pace from the first bell. The 33-year-old Yan, who took the belt from Dvalishvili by unanimous decision in December 2025, withstood a stream of takedown attempts and his piston-like punches left his opponent sporting several red welts on his face at the end of the fight. Facing Yan for the third time in his UFC career, Dvalishvili showed heart and courage, bouncing back repeatedly after shots to the body and head, but Yan kept his cool to pick him off, winning 48-47 on the scorecards of all three judges.

item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro tem 51% dos votos válidos e Lula soma 49%, mostra Datafolha
item.description: O senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) conseguiu abrir uma vantagem numérica sobre o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) na véspera do segundo turno da eleição presidencial, ainda que os dois sigam em empate técnico, mostrou pesquisa Datafolha neste sábado.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: O senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) conseguiu abrir uma vantagem numérica sobre o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) na véspera do segundo turno da eleição presidencial, ainda que os dois sigam em empate técnico, mostrou pesquisa Datafolha neste sábado. Flávio tem 51% dos votos válidos contra 49% de Lula. A margem de erro da pesquisa é de 2 pontos percentuais para mais e para menos. Na sondagem anterior, divulgada na quinta-feira, os dois candidatos estavam numericamente empatados com 50% dos votos válidos, quando não são computados os votos brancos, nulos e os indecisos. No primeiro turno, disputado há três semanas, Flávio terminou na liderança com 47,03% dos votos válidos, contra 45,16% de Lula. Considerando as intenções de voto totais, a pesquisa mostra que Flávio soma 48% contra 47% de Lula. No levantamento anterior, era de 47% a 46% a favor de Flávio. Os que disseram que votarão em branco, anularão o voto ou não votarão em nenhum dos dois passaram a 3%, ante 5%, enquanto os indecisos se mantiveram em 2%. O Datafolha ouviu 4.050 eleitores entre sexta-feira e este sábado.

item.title: Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
item.description: Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Stargardter
item.content:encoded: Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter. Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration. The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who [USN:L1N3ZM12Y TEXT:"oversees Brazil policy"], and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported. Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said. In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said. After Bolsonaro received a [USN:S0N3UJ08N TEXT:"27-year sentence in September 2025"], the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said. Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department. State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections." Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests. Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration. Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed." SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of " free speech diplomacy ," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies. The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions. Moraes did not respond to a comment request. Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America. Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court. Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power. Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption. Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so. Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment. Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said. The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts. A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy." TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime. Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups. In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time. Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those [USN:S0N3ON011 TEXT:"announced against Mexican cartels"] in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said. Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees. The State Department announced the designation the following day. Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision. BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil. Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said. Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS (JBSS.O) - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down. Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March [USN:S0N3ZG01R TEXT:"Brazil barred Beattie"] from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity. Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory. "Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

item.title: Lindt got chocolate price hikes wrong, chairman says after CEO's ouster
item.description: 'We overestimated how much we could raise prices without hurting demand.'
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Lindt & Sprüngli (LISN.S) has struggled because it misjudged how consumers would respond to price increases, the chair of the Swiss chocolate maker said, days after the company [USN:L6N4650EX TEXT:"ousted"] its CEO over concerns about its performance. In an interview with the NZZ am Sonntag newspaper, Executive Chairman Ernst Tanner said the firm, whose shares have tumbled more than 25% this year after recent outlook [USN:L8N45L05W TEXT:"cuts"], was largely suffering because it had misread the market in Germany. "We misjudged how customers would respond to price increases. After cocoa prices reached historic highs from 2024 onwards, we wanted to pass on those additional costs. In doing so, we overestimated how much we could raise prices without hurting demand," he said. "For some consumers, our products clearly became too expensive in recent months." "Lindt & Sprüngli as a whole, however, is not in crisis," Tanner added, arguing the company's shares are now undervalued. "In the Americas and the Far East, we'll achieve our growth targets of 6% to 8% this year as well." Tanner, 80, who was CEO from 1993 to 2016 and has been chairman for over three decades, rejected the suggestion that he should stand down, saying he had important work to do to get Lindt back on track. "Once that's been achieved, I look forward to turning to the next phase of my life," he said. Tanner said the company had already cut some prices as it seeks to lift sales volumes, and would have more scope to do so once cocoa prices returned to more normal levels. He said there would not be group-wide job cuts and that the firm wanted to keep growing. Still, he said thrift was required and that bonuses would be affected in the Germany-Switzerland-Austria region as targets had been missed.

item.title: Trump announces Audi will build $4 billion US factory in Georgia
item.description: US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that Audi plans to build a $4 billion assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually, as he seeks to convince Americans to back Republicans in the November midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that Audi plans to build a $4 billion assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually, as he seeks to convince Americans to back Republicans in the November midterm elections. Trump, who has pressured automakers to move production to the United States and has raised tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and parts, made the announcement at a rally in Perry, near Macon in central Georgia, where Volkswagen's premium subsidiary intends to build its first US assembly plant. Last year, Trump's tariffs dealt Audi a €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion) blow as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico. Georgia has competitive election races for US Senate and governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy. Critics say they have boosted vehicle prices and that the trade uncertainty has delayed some automaker investments. "We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia," Audi CEO Gernot Doellner said at the event. "This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market." In Germany, meanwhile, there has been [USN:L8N4690LO TEXT:"increasing tension"] between Volkswagen management and workers over massive job cuts in the carmaker's home market, including possible plant closures in light of rising costs and stiff Asian competition. "It is right and necessary to better tap into the US market via a new plant," said Christiane Benner, head of the IG Metall union and Volkswagen's deputy supervisory board chair. "However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set out." She said a final decision on the investment would have to be taken by Volkswagen's supervisory board. Olaf Lies, state premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an opportunity provided German workers also benefit. "Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them," he said. REPUBLICAN SAYS TARIFFS BROUGHT AUDI PLANT TO UNITED STATES Audi said the investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with production starting in the early 2030s, Audi said. The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official told Reuters. Audi also plans to build 25,000 vehicles a year in neighboring South Carolina, the official said. Some of the vehicles, now built in Europe, would be exported, the official added. Those vehicles will be assembled at a $2 billion plant of VW's off-road brand Scout Motors that is under construction in Blythewood, near the state capital, Columbia, the official said. "We regard the region as a key market for profitable growth," Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said. "A potential Audi plant in the US would create further conditions for this." Trump has cut government incentives for electric vehicles, causing a significant reduction in EV and battery production in the country. US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year. A gold Audi with manufacturer license plates was parked outside Trump's rally. US Senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, said late on Saturday that "with this investment, Audi will build all of their SUVs exclusively in the US". He said the Audi plant "would never have happened without tariffs, without common sense regulations and without eliminating California’s ability to regulate fuel economy standards". Audi sales have fallen for two consecutive years and slid 7% in the first half of 2026 as fierce competition in China and US tariffs hit demand. Audi's US sales are down 16% this year. Audi's Neckarsulm plant in southwest Germany is one of four German Volkswagen plants facing possible closure after 2030. In July, Japan's Toyota (7203.T) said it would spend $3.6 billion to build a 2.5 million square foot (232,000 square metre) truck assembly line on its manufacturing campus in San Antonio, Texas, and shift some truck production to the US from Mexico. The Japanese automaker said the expansion would be completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs. Honda Motor (7267.T) is considering building a US assembly plant but has warned it may not unless the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement on trade is extended. South Korea's Hyundai said last year that if it had certainty about USMCA, it "would immediately unlock over $20 billion in new American investments".

item.title: Tristan Luneau pushes Ducks past resurgent Flyers
item.description: Tristan Luneau had a goal and two assists as the visiting Anaheim Ducks snapped a five-game losing streak with a 5-4 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Tristan Luneau had a goal and two assists as the visiting Anaheim Ducks snapped a five-game losing streak with a 5-4 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers on Saturday. Leo Carlsson chipped in with a goal and an assist against the team that signed him to a five-year, $90 million offer sheet over the summer. Anaheim ultimately matched the deal, making the 21-year-old the highest paid player in the league. Matvei Michkov scored his seventh and eighth goals for Philadelphia, which had won three straight since losing its first nine contests. Porter Martone had a goal and an assist and Tyson Foerster also scored for the Flyers, while Trevor Zegras recorded two assists against his former team. The Ducks took a 5-3 lead with two goals early in the third period. The go-ahead tally was Luneau's first of the season on a seemingly harmless shot that snuck past Joseph Woll two minutes into the period. Beckett Sennecke then created a two-goal lead when he tipped home a feed from Carlsson for a power-play goal at 7:10. Just over a minute later, Michkov poked in a loose puck to bring the Flyers within 5-4. Philadelphia never seriously threatened down the stretch, despite getting a power play for the final 40.7 seconds. Anaheim's Sam Colangelo and A.J. Greer took simultaneous minor penalties with 6:19 left in the first period -- a sequence that led to two Philadelphia goals. Michkov scored first on a shot through traffic with the Flyers skating 5-on-3 at 13:59, and then Martone scored on a great setup from Travis Sanheim on the ensuing 5-on-4 at 15:02. The Ducks got on the board midway through the second period, as Cutter Gauthier stole the puck behind the net and found Carlsson for a goal. Greer tied it less than five minutes later, but the Flyers answered right back. Foerster gave the hosts a 3-2 lead with a short-handed goal against Lukas Dostal at 15:04. But the visitors responded just over a minute later as Judd Caulfield tipped in a centering pass by Alex Killorn to create a 3-3 tie. Anaheim received a power play late in the second period, but Woll held firm with back-to-back terrific saves against Gauthier. Woll finished with 21 saves for the Flyers, while Dostal turned aside 28 shots for the Ducks. --Field Level Media

item.title: US Justice Dept demands California counties help identify suspected noncitizen voters
item.description: Less than two weeks before US midterm elections, the US Justice Department has warned election officials across California they could be targets of federal "scrutiny" if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls and set aside their mail ballots pending citizenship checks.
item.dc:creator: David Brunnstrom
item.content:encoded: Less than two weeks before US midterm elections, the US Justice Department has warned election officials across California they could be targets of federal "scrutiny" if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls and set aside their mail ballots pending citizenship checks. According to letters dated Friday, local officials were given 48 hours to help determine the citizenship status of individuals on federal government lists. The Justice Department shared with Reuters texts of six of the letters on Saturday, which were signed by Bilal Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California. He warned counties that continuing to process ballots from individuals on the list without verifying citizenship status risked "significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure." On Saturday, California's attorney general accused the Justice Department of "politicizing and weaponizing the law" to attack President Donald Trump's perceived enemies. Officials who knowingly counted ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens risked becoming "aiders and abettors to a federal crime," Essayli wrote. Each letter includes local statistics drawn from a previously distributed list of 20,000 people who the Justice Department alleges are noncitizens registered to vote. For those whose "citizenship status cannot be confirmed, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate — not cancel — those individuals' vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined," Essayli wrote. The Justice Department said it identified 1,754 suspected noncitizens registered to vote in Orange County, 1,355 in Riverside County, 1,133 in San Bernardino County, 334 in Ventura County, 180 in Santa Barbara County and 63 in San Luis Obispo County. Another letter separately shared by Contra Costa County listed "407 likely aliens" registered. "This letter came to us 11 days before Election Day with an unenforceable 48-hour deadline," said Dawn Kruger, a spokesperson for Contra Costa County’s Elections Department, adding: "Our office is conducting this election in accordance with federal and state laws and that is what we will continue to do." Versions of the letters were sent to all 58 California counties, according to the New York Times. In the run-up to the midterms, the Justice Department has ramped up prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. The White House has also pushed federal agencies to accelerate their review of at least 47 state voter rolls obtained by the Department of Homeland Security, according to an internal email seen by Reuters. On October 16, the Justice Department warned Los Angeles County and California election officials they could be liable as [USN:L1N46212B TEXT:"abettors of a federal crime"] if they count mail ballots returned by more than 20,000 people the Trump administration says are probably noncitizens. That warning came the day after the Trump administration [USN:L6N46117W TEXT:"filed a lawsuit"] asking a federal judge to block the state from counting mail ballots from those 20,000 people. The Justice Department on Thursday asked the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals [USN:L6N46900Y TEXT:"to intervene"] in the case. On Saturday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the Justice Department acted at Trump's direction. "It is once again the United States Department of Justice politicizing and weaponizing the law to attack its enemies, and it is completely improper," he told MS Now. California officials have rejected the Justice Department's demand to set aside those ballots, saying the federal government has not provided sufficient information about how it identified the alleged noncitizens. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber has accused the administration of attempting to unlawfully access protected voter data and purge voter rolls, saying such efforts undermine confidence in elections.

item.title: Protests sweep Italian cities amid heavy security presence, some violence reported
item.description: Authorities deployed a heavy police presence and many shops closed as a precaution.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Protests against war and rising living costs took place in major Italian cities on Saturday, with some incidents of violence, a week after unrest erupted across the country. Authorities deployed a heavy police presence and many shops closed as a precaution against possible damage. The demonstrations, [USN:L8N4650S6 TEXT:"which followed clashes last weekend"] in which protesters fought with police, looted shops and vandalised property, were violent in Turin, Rome and Bologna, with clashes between officers and demonstrators. They were largely peaceful in Milan. Reuters witnesses did not observe any shops being looted or property vandalised. After calls for further demonstrations circulated on social media this week, authorities made extensive security arrangements and deployed large numbers of police officers to prevent a repeat of last weekend's violence. Earlier on Saturday, Italian police said they had detained a person allegedly linked to organising the "October 17 Movement" — last weekend's protests — and had taken them to police headquarters in Milan for questioning.

item.title: Nigeria's Tinubu launches re-election campaign as economic pain tests support
item.description: President Bola Tinubu formally launched his campaign for a second term on Saturday in the northern city of Kaduna, where he sought to convince voters that painful economic reforms are beginning to pay off despite a lingering cost-of-living crisis.
item.dc:creator: Camillus Eboh, Ben Ezeamalu
item.content:encoded: President Bola Tinubu formally launched his campaign for a second term on Saturday in the northern city of Kaduna, where he sought to convince voters that painful economic reforms are beginning to pay off despite a lingering cost-of-living crisis. Tinubu, 74, faces a contest ahead of a January 16 election that is likely to be dominated by the economy and security. His main challengers include former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, who finished second and third respectively in 2023. By midday, thousands of supporters of the president's All Progressives Congress party had filled much of the 10,000-capacity Ranchers Bees Stadium, with more arriving as the rally got underway. "Thank you for this massive showing up. It is a promise. Come 2027, January 16, you must go out massively and elect me again," Tinubu told the crowd. OPPOSITION CREATED PROBLEMS, SAYS TINUBU Since taking office in 2023, Tinubu has scrapped [USN:S8N36204O TEXT:"fuel subsidies"], devalued the [USN:S8N362046 TEXT:"naira"] and introduced other reforms credited with improving public finances, foreign reserves and investor sentiment. But the measures have also fuelled Nigeria's worst cost-of-living crisis in a generation. Petrol prices rose to about 1,400 naira ($1.05) a litre in Lagos and Abuja in September and as much as 1,500 naira in parts of northern Nigeria, adding to pressure on household budgets. Tinubu dismissed opposition complaints about hunger and poverty, arguing that his rivals created those problems. "They created the hunger. They created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it." Phrank Shaibu, a spokesperson for the Atiku campaign, told Reuters the president was attempting to dodge responsibility. "Mr President, blaming the opposition for hunger is either delusion or a staggering case of political amnesia," he said. Security will provide [USN:L6N44N0Z4 TEXT:"another test"]. Nigeria continues to battle armed bandits and kidnappers in the northwest and a 17-year Islamist insurgency in the northeast, where militants have stepped up attacks on military positions. Tinubu nevertheless enters the race with a formidable political machine. His camp says he has the backing of 32 of Nigeria's 36 state governors, potentially giving him an unprecedented organisational advantage, although past elections have shown governors cannot always deliver their states to presidential candidates. His toughest electoral test could come in [USN:L6N434151 TEXT:"the north"], where Atiku, a veteran northern politician with an established support base, will seek to erode the president's vote. Tinubu has said he will not attend campaign rallies in all 36 states as he needs to remain focused on governing. The party's proposed timetable has him personally attending rallies in 12 states, culminating in a major closing rally in his home state of Lagos on January 9. ($1 = 1,330.6400 naira)

item.title: Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, intelligence memo warns
item.description: The alert came after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week.
item.dc:creator: Humeyra Pamuk, Enas Alashray
item.content:encoded: Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, and lethal plots by Tehran against American citizens have reached "advanced stages", a senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warned in a memo seen by Reuters. The alert from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton came after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week in response to intensified attacks by Iran-allied Houthi forces. Those attacks on one front of the nearly eight-month-old regional conflict triggered by the Iran war have coincided with [USN:L8N4682UH TEXT:"a rise in attacks"] on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this month, sources told Reuters Iran was preparing a [USN:L8N45M1N4 TEXT:"more forceful response"] if the United States resumes large-scale military attacks on its territory. "Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel," Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a message dated October 23. "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," he added. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was also copied in on the unclassified memo which was first reported by Axios. The State Department on Wednesday [USN:L6N46718Z TEXT:"ordered"] non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave US diplomatic missions in Saudi Arabia and planned to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the region, US officials told Reuters. On Saturday, the US State Department updated travel advisories for more than a dozen countries across the Gulf and Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Israel, citing an increased threat from Iran-aligned Houthis. "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a US official said. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region," the official said. The Restricted Operations Status provides the State Department more flexibility in personnel decisions without having to publicly announce a change in the status of a mission. The Iran war is a week away from entering its ninth month and has significantly weighed on the approval ratings of US President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections on November 3.

item.title: Lula se despede da campanha com multidão na Paulista em ato "sem nada igual" na vida
item.description: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) encerrou neste sábado a oitava campanha presidencial de sua vida com o que disse ser o maior ato político que já fez na vida, uma caminhada com uma multidão de apoiadores na Avenida Paulista, na véspera do segundo turno da disputa contra o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).
item.dc:creator: Lisandra Paraguassu
item.content:encoded: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) encerrou neste sábado a oitava campanha presidencial de sua vida com o que disse ser o maior ato político que já fez na vida, uma caminhada com uma multidão de apoiadores na Avenida Paulista, na véspera do segundo turno da disputa contra o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). “Eu participo aqui da campanha há muitos anos das 'Diretas Já' e nada foi igual o dia de hoje”, disse Lula a jornalistas no final da manifestação. Durante o ato, o presidente chegou a deixar o carro onde estava para subir no caminhão da imprensa para ver a extensão da manifestação de cima. De acordo com a assessoria da campanha de Lula, dois milhões de pessoas estiveram no ato. Não há número oficial de presentes estimado pela polícia. No que foi seu último ato em uma campanha presidencial, aos 80 anos, Lula conseguiu reunir uma multidão que incluiu desde crianças de colo a idosos, muitos chorando ao ver o presidente passar. Gisele Passos, empresária de 61 anos, era uma das milhares de pessoas que saíram de casa para a despedida de Lula em campanha. Visivelmente emocionada, ela disse que sua admiração por Lula é antiga. “Ele está do nosso lado desde sempre”, disse. “Essa movimentação toda me emocionada muito.” Ao chegar à Paulista, Lula afirmou que o povo tomou nas mãos a sua campanha neste segundo turno. "Neste segundo turno, a sociedade brasileira resolveu assumir a responsabilidade de dizer que a eleição não é uma coisa de partido político, que a eleição é de pessoas que se preocupam com o país, que se preocupam com o dia a dia de outras pessoas, de pessoas que não querem que miliciano vá para o Palácio do Planalto", afirmou. Mais cedo, no Rio de Janeiro, Lula também reuniu uma multidão para uma caminhada na praia de Copacabana. "Hoje nós temos um exército de democratas neste país maior que o Exército chinês, maior que o Exército russo e maior que o Exército americano que é o Exército do Lula, que vai chegar a 13 milhões de soldados e soldadas amanhã", afirmou. "E vamos ganhar as eleições por uma simples razão: é verdade que o povo quer mudança, e o povo quer mudança para melhor, o povo quer mudança para frente. O povo não quer retroceder e não está longe da nossa memória o que aconteceu no mandato dessa gente nesse país". Lula se referia ao canal de WhatsApp Exército do Lula, criado pelo deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG), no qual o parlamentar passa a apoiadores "missões" para colocar Lula em destaque nas redes sociais e para fazer críticas a Flávio. A fala de Lula sobre a participação popular no segundo turno da campanha vem depois de uma série de críticas à campanha petista no primeiro turno, de dentro e de fora do PT e inclusive do próprio Lula, que em reunião logo após a primeira rodada disse que a campanha até o dia 4 de outubro foi a "menos organizada" de que participou desde 1989. Pesquisas eleitorais divulgadas neste sábado mantiveram o empate técnico entre Lula e Flávio, mas com vantagem numérica para o senador de oposição de um a dois pontos.

item.title: UAE's Ras Al Khaimah shuts all beaches as neighbours grapple with oil spill
item.description: Residents reported unusual odours in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE's environment ministry said they posed no health risks.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after an offshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighbouring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah. The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given. The United Arab Emirates [USN:L1N469029 TEXT:"said on Friday"] that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment. All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said. The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions. Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE's northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran , attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict's environmental fallout. Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts' planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island. The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE's first commercial gaming licence in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027. Wynn said in March [USN:L4N44122B TEXT:"it had resumed"] construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East. Residents reported unusual odours in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE's environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday. UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill.

item.title: Around 1,200 Palestinians are displaced in Hebron as Israel begins military operation
item.description: The Palestinian Authority criticised the operation as a "collective punishment".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Israeli military forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said on Saturday, a day after a Palestinian attack [USN:L1N4690KO TEXT:"killed two Israeli"] soldiers. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday had said the military would launch a large-scale operation after the soldiers were killed when two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at a military checkpoint near the city. The Israeli military said the gunmen were shot dead. They also said the operation in the Al-Jaladah and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods near the military checkpoint at the entrance of Hebron was to search for militants and weapons. In a statement, it also said the military would carry out demolitions. The Palestinian Authority criticised the operation as a "collective punishment". Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, the head of Hebron's municipality, said around 1,300 faced losing their homes in addition to the 1,200 already displaced. He also said the Israeli operations were motivated by parliamentary elections on Tuesday when Netanyahu's right-wing coalition may lose his majority, opinion polls show. "Netanyahu and the radical ministers in his government are trying to win as many votes as possible from the settlers," Al-Jabari said. The non-governmental organisation the Palestinian Prisoners' Club said Israeli forces had arrested around 70 Palestinians on Friday and Saturday. Israeli officials have not commented on any arrests. NETANYAHU'S GOVERNMENT HAS PRESIDED OVER EXPANSION OF SETTLEMENTS Al-Jabari said the military had demolished shops, factories, homes, and roads in Hebron and that the response was disproportionate and unjustified. Residents in Hebron told Reuters that the military expelled many people with no connection to the Palestinian attackers. "We are calling on officials to stand by us because we are not involved in any of this. There are children. We are isolated; we don’t do anything. This is all arbitrary,” said Majdi Nasser, one of those driven from his home. Residents told Reuters they saw Israeli soldiers marking homes with a black X after their Palestinian occupants had been forced to leave. It was not immediately clear what the X mark meant. Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid [USN:L6N44Y077 TEXT:"expansion"] of settlements, deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Across the West Bank, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement. Yousef Mur, a resident of the Palestinian town of Yatta, said the closures meant he was unable to reach Jerusalem with his daughter for her cancer treatment. "The situation is bad, and we are suffering. When we tried to cross, they fired stun grenades towards us, and my girl got scared on the way. They fired stun grenades towards people. The situation is very difficult," Mur said. (This story has been refiled to remove the repeated word 'when' in paragraph 2.)

item.title: Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
item.description: In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Jacob Bogage
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress. In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks. Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country: TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “[USN:L1N45M10K TEXT:"bad job"]” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low [USN:S0N4310A5 TEXT:"poverty rate"], low [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"unemployment,"] record highs in the [USN:L6N45S0IV TEXT:"stock market"] and cheaper prices for some food items. But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses. Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends. The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people. “Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family." RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory. Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday. Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election. Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa. Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine. TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity. But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues. "I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special." The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens. At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty. Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday. Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them. FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods. But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade. “What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday. Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran. “They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world. TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic. This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton. At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.” “Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said. Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old." Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents. Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton. "Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't." That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

item.title: Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests across France
item.description: The interior minister mobilized 70,000 police nationwide, 10,000 more than on October 17, when vandalism and looting raised questions about the government's ability to maintain order.
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Yann Tessier, Crispian Balmer
item.content:encoded: Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of [USN:L1N46608H TEXT:"last week's unrest"]. The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high. The main demonstration took place on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality. The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon at a group of around 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed on a cold, rainy evening. In France's second city, Marseille, youths set fire to rubbish bins to block roads, and hurled rocks and bottles at security forces. Police said several stores, including two jewellery shops, were ransacked. Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse. "In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment trouble. PARIS IN LOCKDOWN Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on October 17. Nunez told reporters the violence was less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage. "What changed was anticipation," he said. He also said far-right activists had sought confrontations with leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, opening a potential new front in the disturbances. Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers [USN:L2N46A00I TEXT:"boarding up storefronts"], [USN:L5N46A022 TEXT:"museums closing their doors"] and more than 20 metro stations shut. Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend. "There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris. Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated. "Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans. PROTESTS RIPPLE ACROSS EUROPE The nationwide disorder began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris last month to denounce school conditions. It swiftly broadened into a wider protest against the government's economic policies and inspired demonstrations in neighbouring countries. On Saturday [USN:L6N46A05C TEXT:"Belgian police"] used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, with protests also taking place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend, [USN:L2N46A02Y TEXT:"and in Albania"]. Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world's richest nations. "Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters. FAR-RIGHT PARTY HOLDS CONGRESS Many demonstrators accused the government of overreacting to last week's turmoil, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants. "We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student. "My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added. The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city. A [USN:L6N4690NC TEXT:"shooting"] west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl. "We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

item.title: Trump foreign policy hits voters in the pocketbook, imperiling Republicans in midterms
item.description: Voters are drawing that connection directly.
item.dc:creator: Matt Spetalnick
item.content:encoded: Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters’ choices. But this time, with Donald Trump’s war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue. As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress. Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame Trump's policies"] for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings. Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader’s handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome. The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago. “The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies,” said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. “Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this.” POLITICS DRIVING FOREIGN POLICY With Trump’s [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"approval ratings"] touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living. That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections. Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"Russian diesel"] exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine. He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on [USN:L1N46203J TEXT:"Russian refineries"] as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago. At the same time, he has promised not to order any [USN:FWN45U1SW TEXT:"new attack"] on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections. Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003. Some Republican candidates have [USN:L4N45N1R0 TEXT:"distanced themselves"] from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine. For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the [USN:L8N46515R TEXT:"diplomatic stalemate"], senior Iranian officials have told Reuters. Defending the administration's approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear." ‘IT’S THE ECONOMY, STUPID’ Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House. And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - “it’s the economy, stupid,” as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters’ choices. Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs. Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey “finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions.” Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the [USN:L1N45G0ZJ TEXT:"limits of US power"] have been increasingly exposed, analysts say. LEGISLATIVE BALANCE OF POWER IN PLAY Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"gain control"] of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play. For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term. But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit. Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made. “For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington. Analysts say Trump's handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way -- or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

item.title: US has for years asked Musk to alter Starlink service in Ukraine, Middle East, sources say
item.description: The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe.
item.dc:creator: Erin Banco, Joey Roulette
item.content:encoded: Well before the throttling this month of Ukraine's military access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system, the Biden and Trump administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn its Starlink service on or off in various countries, according to six former senior US officials familiar with the matter. During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials. Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. All of the people spoke on condition of anonymity. The previous US requests about Starlink access are being reported here for the first time. The recent blowup over restrictions to Ukraine's use of SpaceX satellite services has raised questions about the ties between the US government and Musk, whose company owns systems vital to the US military and to US allies. The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy. The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe, some of whom argue that Europe must develop its own military satellite communications capabilities because no viable short-term alternative currently exists. STARSHIELD RESTRICTIONS HOBBLE UKRAINE MILITARY Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that his country's access to Starshield, the military version of the Starlink system, had been intentionally limited, interfering with the performance of the country’s military drones. He also said the speeds were reduced for Starlink, which Ukraine uses for some military activities including defense against Russian missile attacks. Reuters has reported that [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"the order to throttle Starshield"] came from inside the White House. The Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not said whether it gave the order. The White House, contacted for comment, referred Reuters to Trump's remarks on Friday, when he said he had not spoken with Musk about Starlink access issues for Ukraine and that "if there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out." Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Ukraine's priority is "to have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it." SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment, although Musk said in a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).” Democratic US Representative Jason Crow called on Friday for clarity about the recent changes to Ukraine's satellite service, saying there are risks to the US dependence on SpaceX. "Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Crow said. For Ukraine, the Starlink internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival to the capabilities of SpaceX's products. Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio jamming, are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine. MUSK'S INFLUENCE RAISES UNCERTAINTY Musk's role as the strong-willed CEO of a company with outsized influence over US national security has at times raised questions over who is making decisions about SpaceX's satellite services. The SpaceX CEO is "supposed to be a business executive, with government contracts, and he's essentially making huge foreign policy decisions," said Armand Musey, president of Summit Ridge Group, a satellite industry consultancy. "He's sufficiently ambiguous of a person that you don't know if his decisions are sort of his personal quirks, or it's because there's an influence elsewhere that's impacting him," Musey said. In previous years, Musk has moved to limit Ukraine’s access to Starlink. In 2022, according to Reuters reporting , Musk ordered SpaceX personnel to cut Starlink coverage in areas Ukraine was trying to retake, a move that surprised White House officials. Musk has said publicly that he refused a 2022 Ukrainian request to activate his satellite network in Crimea's port city of Sevastopol to aid an attack on Russia's fleet there, saying he feared complicity in a major act of war. The Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy, five of the former officials said. Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink’s availability, they said. They added that discussions between the government and SpaceX, which usually included Pentagon and White House officials, often focused on preventing groups such as the Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon from using Starlink terminals. Biden officials several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals — hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries. In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah militants in southern Lebanon, intelligence officials told the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah could have gained access to Starlink terminals. Officials had similar concerns about the Houthis in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Iran-linked group, five of the officials said. In both cases, the administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of the terminals were deactivated, said two of the officials. In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals. Soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Biden officials pushed SpaceX to expand Starlink use for the Ukrainian military, said two of the former officials. In a separate instance, the Biden administration asked SpaceX to turn on Starlink in Iran during a protest movement launched in September 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini, an Iranian arrested for not wearing her hijab properly, according to one of the former officials. Starlink terminals were moved into the country with the help of the administration, said the official, who declined to say how many were transferred. The Trump administration took a similar step earlier this year and discussed with Musk and SpaceX getting Starlink terminals into Iran and activated following US-Israeli strikes in the country in June 2025 and again in February 2026, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed that those terminals were turned on. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran. Iran's delegation to the UN did not respond to a request for comment.
